المتحدة في جنوب السودان خلال إحاطة أمام ‏مجلس الأمن الدولي- موقع الأمم المتحدة جوبا-سانا ‏ حذّرت بعثة الأمم المتحدة في جنوب السودان (‏UNMISS‏) من تفاقم الأوضاع الإنسانية والأمنية في البلاد، ‏مشيرة إلى أن نحو 10 ملايين شخص يحتاجون إلى مساعدات إنسانية، فيما يواجه 7.5 ملايين شخص ‏انعدام الأمن الغذائي. ‏ وقالت الممثلة الخاصة للأمين العام للأمم المتحدة ورئيسة البعثة، أنيتا كيكي غبيهو، خلال إحاطة أمام ‏مجلس الأمن الدولي، أمس الثلاثاء: إن القيود على وصول المساعدات الإنسانية ارتفعت بنسبة 38 بالمئة ‏خلال العام الماضي، محذرة من تزايد أعداد المهددين بالمجاعة وتداعيات الجفاف والفيضانات المتوقعة ‏المرتبطة بظاهرة “إل نينيو”.‏ وأضافت أن نحو 1.4 مليون شخص عبروا إلى جنوب السودان منذ اندلاع الحرب في السودان، ما يزيد ‏الضغوط على الاستجابة الإنسانية، في وقت تواجه فيه البلاد تحديات إضافية مرتبطة بتفشي إيبولا في ‏المنطقة.‏ وعلى الصعيد الأمني، أشارت غبيهو إلى استمرار أعمال العنف المجتمعي والانقسامات المحلية والتنافس ‏على الموارد، موضحة أن العنف بين المجتمعات المحلية يشكل أكثر من 60 بالمئة من إجمالي الضحايا ‏المدنيين المسجلين خلال العام الجاري، فيما أسفرت اشتباكات شهدتها مناطق رومبيك وتونج الكبرى الشهر ‏الماضي عن مقتل أكثر من 140 شخصاً.‏ ولفتت إلى أن بعثة الأمم المتحدة ضاعفت مهام حماية العمليات الإنسانية، ما ساعد على إيصال المساعدات ‏المنقذة للحياة إلى أكثر من 321 ألف شخص، رغم القيود التي تواجه حركة البعثة والعاملين في المجال ‏الإنساني.‏ ودعت المسؤولة الأممية جميع الأطراف إلى وقف القتال واحترام وقف إطلاق النار وحماية المدنيين، ‏وضمان وصول المساعدات الإنسانية دون عوائق، إلى جانب إطلاق حوار سياسي شامل للحفاظ على ‏الاستقرار وتنفيذ اتفاق السلام.‏ وتواجه جنوب السودان ضغوطاً إنسانية متزايدة منذ اندلاع الحرب في السودان، مع تدفق مئات الآلاف من ‏اللاجئين والعائدين عبر الحدود، ما زاد الأعباء على الخدمات الأساسية والمجتمعات المحلية، في وقت ‏تعاني فيه البلاد أصلاً من الفقر وانعدام الأمن الغذائي ونقص التمويل الإنساني.‏ قوات الاحتلال تعتقل فلسطينيين اثنين في الضفة الغربية روبيو يحدد شروط ترامب لبدء مرحلتي التفاوض مع إيران عون وترامب يبحثان هاتفياً التطورات في لبنان وتنفيذ بنود السودان تحت التهديد.. هدم وتضييق متصاعد تواجه كنيسة المسيح السودانية في منطقة "مرزوق" بأم درمان تهديداً وشيكاً بالهدم من السلطات المحلية التابعة لسلطة بورتسودان، بذريعة تشييدها على أرض عامة، رغم امتلاك الكنيسة وثائق وسندات قانونية تثبت ملكيتها للأرض منذ أكثر من خمسة عقود. وبحسب تجمع الأجسام المطلبية السودانية "تام"، وصلت سلطات الأراضي إلى مبنى الكنيسة ، من دون إخطار مسبق، وأبلغت المسؤولين بوجود خطة لهدم المبنى المقام بالمربع 59 في منطقة مرزوق. سندات ملكية لا توقف التهديد وقال القس تيا ملاسا كوكو، راعي الكنيسة، إن المبنى شُيد في أواخر ثمانينيات القرن الماضي، وإن قادة الكنيسة قدموا سندات الملكية والوثائق القانونية التي تثبت حقهم في الأرض والمبنى، إلا أن المسؤولين طالبوهم بالتوجه إلى سلطات الأراضي بالمحلية. وأضاف أن السلطات في محلية كرري، صاحبة الاختصاص، أحالتهم بدورها إلى وزارة الشؤون الدينية، التي وجهت أوراقهم إلى إدارة الشؤون الهندسية والتخطيط العمراني، حيث لا تزال المعاملة معلقة منذ أواخر يوليو الماضي من دون حسم. وأوضح راعي الكنيسة أن السلطات منحت الرعية، في البداية، مهلة أسبوعين لتسوية النزاع، ثم مددت المهلة أسبوعاً إضافياً خلال الأسبوع الأول من أغسطس، بينما لا تزال الإجراءات المحلية مستمرة من دون نتيجة نهائية. وحذر القس ملاسا كوكو من أن الكنيسة، التي تخدم نحو 300 شخص، تواجه خطر هدم مبناها في أي وقت، مؤكداً أن قادة الكنيسة يعتبرون ما يحدث استهدافاً لعقيدتهم ومقدساتهم وممتلكاتهم الدينية. عودة المتطرفين.. وعودة التضييق ويقول نشطاء وسياسيون مدنيون إن عودة الحركة الإسلامية السودانية المتحالفة مع الجيش إلى الساحة السياسية، عقب انقلابه على الحكومة المدنية، أعادت معها المتطرفين الإسلاميين وممارسات التضييق على المسيحيين. وفي 25 أكتوبر 2021، أطاح انقلاب عسكري بالحكومة الانتقالية، بدعم من الحركة الإسلامية السودانية (الإخوان)، التي حكمت السودان لثلاثة عقود، وعاد الإسلاميون بعده إلى مفاصل الدولة، خصوصاً الأجهزة الأمنية والمحليات. وعلى مدى أكثر من ثلاثة عقود من حكم النظام السابق، لم تمنح الدولة السودانية أي تصديق لبناء كنيسة، إذ يعود آخر تصريح رسمي إلى عام 1987. وسبق أن قال جاتيكا أموجا دلمان، القيادي بالحركة الشعبية - جبال النوبة، لـ"سكاي نيوز عربية": "منذ وصول الحركة الإسلامية للسلطة عام 1989، بدأ التضييق على المسيحيين والكنائس وتفريغها من الطلاب ودفعهم شمالا نحو معسكرات النزوح، حيث يُعاد إنتاجهم داخل المشروع الإسلاموي". وأضاف دلمان: "مع عودة نظام البشير عادت عملية الاستهداف لدور العبادة للمسيحيين مستمرة". وقال وزير الشؤون الدينية والأوقاف في الحكومة المدنية الانتقالية السابقة التي انقلب عليها الجيش، نصر الدين مُفرّح: "في عام 2020، أعلنت الحكومة الانتقالية الموافقة على بناء 14 كنيسة، في خطوة وصفت آنذاك بأنها محاولة لتصحيح مسار طويل من التقييد، لكن هذه الموافقات لم تر النور بسبب الانقلاب العسكري الذي قام به البرهان مدفوعاً بالإسلاميين". وأضاف مُفرّح: "كان ذلك آخر ما بدا كأنه مسار مختلف، لكنه لم يكتمل". من التضييق إلى القصف والهدم في 15 أبريل 2023، اندلعت الحرب الجارية، ولم تعد أدوات التضييق قرارات إدارية أو قيوداً قانونية، بل تحولت إلى عنف مباشر وقصف من الجو وترهيب في المدن. ويقول الوزير السابق مُفرّح: "هذا المناخ أسهم في تآكل الحدود بين الحرب والسياسة والدين" وبحسب سياسيين ونشطاء ومصادر محلية، وفرت الحرب بيئة مواتية لتحرك الجماعات المتطرفة بعيداً عن الرقابة والمساءلة. ويضيف مُفرّح: "لم يتوقف الاستهداف عند القصف ولا مناطق القتال، بل امتد إلى دور العبادة". وهُدمت 13 كنيسة في الخرطوم ومناطق أخرى منذ خروج قوات الدعم السريع من العاصمة وسيطرة الجيش على المدينة في مارس 2025. وجرى الهدم بذريعة إزالة السكن العشوائي، رغم أن الكنائس المستهدفة كانت قائمة وتواصل أداء شعائرها الدينية، على الرغم من بساطة بنائها. وتسببت هذه العمليات في تهجير أكثر من 35 ألف مسيحي من العاصمة وحدها، بحسب تقديرات مصادر كنسية. وفي صباح الخامس والعشرين من ديسمبر من العام الماضي، ومع احتفالات المسيحيين بعيد الميلاد، قصفت طائرات مسيّرة تابعة للجيش السوداني تجمعاً دينياً في قرية جلود بجبال النوبة، بولاية جنوب كردفان، ما أدى إلى سقوط 31 بين قتيل وجريح. لكن القصف والهدم لم يكونا الشكل الوحيد للاستهداف. ففي مدينة بورتسودان، حيث انتقلت قيادة الجيش بعد اندلاع الحرب، ظهرت تهديدات وعبارات مسيئة بحق المسيحيين. وفي نهاية العام الماضي، قبيل أعياد الميلاد، كُتبت تهديدات وعبارات بالطلاء الأحمر على جدران كنيستين من أقدم دور العبادة متزايدة، وسط مخاوف من عدم استكمال الشروط اللازمة لتنظيم الاستحقاق الانتخابي، وما قد يترتب على ذلك من تعقيدات جديدة في المشهد السياسي بالبلاد. وقال رئيس المركز العربي الأفريقي لثقافة السلام والديمقراطية في السودان، الدكتور محمد مصطفى، إن إجراء الانتخابات في موعدها يواجه تحديات متعددة، تشمل الجوانب الفنية والإجرائية واللوجستية، إلى جانب الأوضاع الأمنية، مشيرًا في حديثه إلى وكالة «سبوتنيك» إلى أهمية تهيئة الظروف المناسبة قبل التوجه إلى صناديق الاقتراع. وأوضح مصطفى أن الانتخابات تمثل استحقاقًا دستوريًا مهمًا وخطوة أساسية لوضع جمهورية جنوب السودان على طريق التحول الديمقراطي، لكنه حذر من أن تنظيمها دون استكمال المتطلبات الضرورية قد يفقدها قيمتها الدستورية، ويجعلها عاملًا إضافيًا لتعميق الخلافات السياسية والتوترات الأمنية. وأشار إلى أن الحزب الحاكم يدرك حجم المخاطر المرتبطة بإجراء الانتخابات في ظل الظروف الحالية، متوقعًا إعادة تقييم الوضع واتخاذ قرار حاسم بشأن الالتزام بالموعد المعلن أو مراجعة الترتيبات القائمة. ودعا مصطفى إلى تغليب الحوار والتوافق بين الأطراف السياسية، معربًا عن أمله في حدوث انفراجة تنهي حالة الجمود، وتدفع الفرقاء إلى الجلوس حول طاولة المفاوضات لاتخاذ قرارات تجنب البلاد مزيدًا من الأزمات. وطرح عددًا من الإجراءات التي يمكن أن تسهم في تهيئة الأجواء السياسية، من بينها إصدار عفو عن المعتقلين السياسيين، ورفع الإقامة الجبرية عن الدكتور رياك مشار، فضلًا عن تأجيل الانتخابات لبضعة أشهر فقط لإتاحة الفرصة أمام الأطراف لاستكمال ما تبقى من بنود اتفاقية السلام المنشط، أو التوصل إلى صيغة توافقية تسمح للجميع بالمشاركة في الانتخابات. وتأتي هذه التطورات في ظل تعثر مسار الانتقال السياسي في جنوب السودان، بعد سنوات من التأجيل الذي حال دون تنظيم أول انتخابات عامة منذ استقلال البلاد عن السودان عام 2011. وكان اتفاق السلام المنشط الموقع عام 2018 قد وضع إطارًا لإنهاء الصراع بين الأطراف المتنازعة، وتشكيل حكومة وحدة وطنية انتقالية تمهد لإجراء الانتخابات، إلا أن تنفيذ عدد من بنوده لا يزال يواجه صعوبات، خصوصًا فيما يتعلق بالترتيبات الأمنية وتوحيد القوات وإعداد الدستور الدائم واستكمال المؤسسات الانتخابية. كما تتزامن التحضيرات الانتخابية مع استمرار الخلافات بين القوى السياسية، وتفاقم التحديات الأمنية والاقتصادية والإنسانية، الأمر الذي يثير تساؤلات حول مدى توافر الظروف القانونية والسياسية والأمنية اللازمة لضمان انتخابات حرة ونزيهة. وبين التمسك بالموعد المحدد والحاجة إلى استكمال متطلبات اتفاق السلام، تواجه السلطات الانتقالية والقوى السياسية اختبارًا مهمًا لتجنب تحول الانتخابات المرتقبة إلى مصدر جديد للصراع والانقسام في جنوب السودان. المصدر: المشهد السوداني وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية سياسة الأخبار تقصي الحقائق اقتصاد دولي اقاليم الرأي English سودان تربيون أخبار السودان وتقارير حصرية لحظة بلحظة الرئيسية اختيار المحرر الحكومة السودانية تجدد اعتراضها للأمم المتحدة على تحليلات الأمن الغذائي اختيار المحرر الحكومة السودانية تجدد اعتراضها للأمم المتحدة على تحليلات الأمن الغذائي 10 نوفمبر 2026 في اختيار المحرر , الأخبار , السودان 0 وزير الزراعة والري بحث مع المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي سبل تعزيز التعاون المشترك و الخرطوم 10 نوفمبر 2026 – نقلت الحكومة السودانية للأمم المتحدة اعتراضها مجدداً على التحليلات المتعلقة بالأمن الغذائي دون أن تكون طرفاً في إعدادها. وفي مطلع نوفمبر الجاري كشفت منظمة الأمم المتحدة لرعاية الطفولة “يونيسف” ومجموعة التغذية، عن تجاوز السودان عتبة الطوارئ التي حددتها منظمة الصحة العالمية عند 15% في 49% من مسوحات التغذية التي أُجريت في السودان خلال عام 2026. ويحتاج 8.4 ملايين سوداني إلى مساعدات التغذية خلال هذا العام، منهم 4.19 ملايين شخص يُتوقع أن يعانوا من سوء التغذية الحاد، من بينهم 824,827 طفلاً، بحسب الأمم المتحدة. لكن الحكومة السودانية ترفض الاعتراف بوجود أزمة غذاء في البلاد. وقالت يونيسف ومجموعة التغذية، في تقرير يغطي الفترة من يناير إلى سبتمبر، إن “18 من أصل 37 مسحاً تغذوياً، بما يعادل 49% من المسوحات، أظهرت انتشاراً لسوء التغذية الحاد عند عتبة الطوارئ، فيما سجلت 7 مسوحات نسباً تبلغ 20% أو أكثر”. وبدأ المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي لوك ليندبيرج، الثلاثاء، سلسلة اجتماعات مع المسؤولين في الحكومة السودانية شملت رئيس الوزراء ووزيري الزراعة والخارجية. وقالت وزارة الزراعة والري السودانية، في بيان صحفي، إن الوزير عصمت قرشي، بحث مع ليندبيرج سبل تعزيز التعاون المشترك وتطوير التدخلات الداعمة للقطاع الزراعي والأمن الغذائي في السودان. وأوضح أن القطاع الزراعي يمضي في مسار التعافي، وأن المزارعين يواصلون الإنتاج رغم ظروف الحرب والتحديات المناخية، مشيراً إلى أن المساحات المزروعة خلال الموسم الحالي تجاوزت 10 ملايين هكتار، بما يعكس قدرة القطاع على الصمود ومواصلة الإنتاج. وأشار الوزير إلى وجود مناطق تعاني من الهشاشة، خاصة التي تسيطر عليها المليشيات المتمردة، وتواجه أوضاعاً إنسانية وإنتاجية صعبة، واصفاً ما يحدث فيها بأنه عمليات تجويع، ومشدداً على ضرورة توجيه التدخلات الإنسانية والتنموية وفق الاحتياجات الفعلية للمجتمعات والمزارعين. وفيما يتعلق بالتصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي (IPC)، “جدد قرشي رفض الحكومة إجراء أو نشر أي تحليلات بشأن الأمن الغذائي في السودان دون مشاركتها”. وشدد على ضرورة احترام السيادة السودانية وضمان مشاركة المؤسسات الحكومية المختصة في جمع البيانات والتحقق منها وتحليلها، مؤكداً انفتاح الحكومة على استكشاف آليات جديدة لتحليل الأمن الغذائي والتغذوي، بما يضمن المهنية والشفافية ودقة المعلومات. ويُعد التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي (IPC) الذي انسحبت منه الحكومة في أواخر ديسمبر 2024 أداة دولية مشتركة لتحليل وتصنيف شدة انعدام الأمن الغذائي وسوء التغذية، استناداً إلى أدلة علمية ومعايير موحدة، ويقسم الأوضاع إلى خمس مراحل، تبدأ من المرحلة الأولى التي تعبر عن انعدام الأمن الغذائي الحاد أو الظروف الطبيعية، وصولاً إلى المرحلة الخامسة التي تمثل المجاعة أو الكارثة الإنسانية. من جانبه، أكد المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي استمرارهم في تقديم المساعدات الإنسانية وتعزيز الشراكات لمواجهة التحديات، لافتاً إلى أن نحو 266 مليون شخص حول العالم يواجهون مستويات حادة من انعدام الأمن الغذائي، وأن النزاعات تمثل أحد أبرز أسباب تفاقم هذه الأوضاع. وكشف عن تمكن البرنامج من الوصول إلى نحو 600 ألف سوداني وتقديم المساعدات لهم، مؤكداً أن تعزيز الشراكة والتعاون مع الحكومة السودانية يمثل عاملاً أساسياً لضمان نجاح البرامج وتحقيق أثر أكبر على أرض الواقع. وكان رئيس الوزراء كامل إدريس قد التقى أيضاً المدير التنفيذي لبرنامج الأغذية العالمي، لوك ليندبرج، الذي أعرب في تصريح صحفي عن شكره لحكومة السودان على حُسن الاستقبال خلال زيارته الأولى للبلاد بصفته مديراً تنفيذياً للبرنامج، موضحاً أنه عقد خلال الزيارة اجتماعات وصفها بالمثمرة مع وزير الخارجية، ووزير الزراعة والري. الكلمات: الأمن الغذائي التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل الخرطوم السودان السودان تحت نيران المسيّرات.. قتلى في دارفور وهجمات على منشآت حيوية وأضاف أن سكان السودان "يتحدثون عن 3 أمور: الأمان والتعليم والمياه، والطائرات المسيّرة المسلحة تسلبهم هذه الأمور الثلاثة". وقد أسفرت الحرب الدائرة منذ أبريل/نيسان 2023 بين قوات الدعم السريع والجيش السوداني عن مقتل أكثر من 200 ألف شخص، بحسب تقديرات العاملين في المجال الإنساني، وتسببت في أكبر أزمة جوع ونزوح في العالم. ويعتمد طرفا النزاع بشكل متزايد على الضربات البعيدة المدى بمسيّرات قادرة على التحليق لمئات الكيلومترات. وقُتل أكثر من 1100 شخص في هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة في أنحاء السودان خلال النصف الأول من العام الجاري، وفق الأمم المتحدة. تفاقم الأزمة الإنسانية وأوضح إلدر أن تزايد استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة لاستهداف البنية التحتية المدنية يفاقم أيضا تداعيات موجة الجفاف التي تضرب السودان، وحذّر من أن "الطائرات المسيّرة والجفاف يطبقان على أطفال السودان من كل جانب". وفي تشرين الأول/أكتوبر وحده، تعرضت محطات توليد الكهرباء في مختلف أنحاء البلاد لما لا يقل عن 15 ضربة بطائرات مسيّرة، وفق إلدر. إقرأ أيضاً سياسة - السريع , السودان , دولي , شمال كردفان 0 جميس إلدر يجمع متبقي ألعاب وكتب من مستودع يونيسف الذي تضرر جراء هجوم بمسيرة على مدينة الأبيض في 20 سبتمبر 2026.- صورة ليونيسيف الخرطوم 10 نوفمبر 2026 – قال متحدث باسم منظمة الأمم المتحدة لرعاية الطفولة “يونيسيف”، الثلاثاء، إن ضربات الطائرات المسيّرة تسببت في مقتل وإصابة ثلثي الأطفال ضحايا الحرب في السودان خلال العام الحالي. وبرز استخدام الطائرات المسيّرة كاتجاه تصعيدي في قصف الأسواق والمستشفيات ومحطات الكهرباء ومصادر المياه ومواقع النزوح، وسط تزايد وتيرة استخدامها خلف خطوط النزاع المندلع منذ أبريل 2023. وقال المتحدث باسم يونيسيف جيمس إلدر، في مؤتمر صحفي عُقد في قصر الأمم المتحدة بجنيف بعد زيارته السودان، إن “الطائرات المسيّرة تسببت في ثلثي حالات سقوط الأطفال بين قتيل وجريح خلال هذا العام”. وأوضح أن المسيّرات نقلت الحرب إلى مناطق كانت آمنة في السابق. وأشار إلى أن الشهر السابق شهد تعرض 15 محطة كهرباء للقصف، معتبراً أن هذه الهجمات، التي امتدت جغرافياً ونُفذت بوتيرة متسارعة، تمثل تصعيداً خطيراً في استهداف البنية التحتية المدنية. وأضاف: “دعوني أوضح لماذا يشكل اجتماع الطائرات المسيّرة والجفاف خطراً مميتاً على الأطفال. تعني الكهرباء توفير المياه. فعندما تتعرض محطة للقصف، تتوقف مضخات المياه وتتوقف عمليات معالجة المياه، وتُضطر الأسر إلى اللجوء إلى بدائل مكلفة وغير آمنة. وتنتشر الأمراض”. وبيّن أن استهداف محطات الكهرباء يهدد مرافق التبريد التي تحافظ على صلاحية اللقاحات والأدوية، كما يحرم المزارعين من إمكانية ري محاصيلهم، في ظل النقص الحاد والخانق في الوقود، مما يجعل الغذاء بعيد المنال أمام أعداد متزايدة من الأسر. وفي 24 أكتوبر، قال مفوض الأمم المتحدة السامي لحقوق الإنسان، فولكر تورك، إن 306 سودانيين قُتلوا وأُصيب المئات جراء هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة خلال الأسابيع الثلاثة الأولى من أكتوبر. ورصد مكتب الأمم المتحدة لحقوق الإنسان، بحسب ما أعلنه في 4 سبتمبر الماضي، مقتل 1120 مدنياً نتيجة ضربات بطائرات مسيّرة، بما يمثل أكثر من 80% من إجمالي وفيات المدنيين. وتحدث التصنيف المرحلي المتكامل للأمن الغذائي، في 13 أكتوبر الماضي، عن رصد أكثر من 170 غارة جوية أو حادثة نهب أو اشتباك مسلح في أسواق كردفان خلال العام الحالي، مع تركز النزاع على المجتمعات التي تمتلك الماشية، ومجتمعات الرعاة، والتجمعات الزراعية. وأفاد المتحدث بأن ضربات المسيّرات تحدث رغم التوقعات بأن يعاني نحو 825 ألف طفل دون سن الخامسة من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم هذا العام، وهو النوع الذي قد يؤدي إلى الوفاة. وقال جيمس إلدر إن يونيسيف وشركاءها تمكنوا من علاج مئات الآلاف من الأطفال المصابين بأخطر أشكال سوء التغذية فتكاً، إضافة إلى توفير الرعاية الصحية لأكثر من 2. 5 مليون شخص، وتطعيم ملايين الأطفال ضد الأمراض الفتاكة. وأوضح أن يونيسيف أصلحت أنظمة المياه وحولتها إلى العمل بالطاقة الشمسية، ما ساعد على استمرار تدفق المياه الآمنة لنحو 8 ملايين شخص، كما ساعدت ملايين الأطفال على العودة إلى التعلم، فضلاً عن توفير خدمات الحماية والصحة النفسية والدعم النفسي والاجتماعي لنحو 1. 5 مليون طفل وأسرة. ويُقدّر قطاع التغذية التابع للأمم المتحدة أن يحتاج 8.4 مليون من الأطفال دون سن الخامسة والنساء الحوامل والمرضعات في 2026 إلى مساعدات التغذية، منهم نحو 5 ملايين طفل دون سن الخامسة و3.4 ملايين من الحوامل والمرضعات. ويحتاج 4. 19 مليون شخص إلى خدمات علاج سوء التغذية الحاد خلال هذا العام، من بينهم نحو 825 ألف طفل دون سن الخامسة يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد الوخيم، و2.76 مليون شخص يعانون من سوء التغذية الحاد المتوسط، و599,681 من الحوامل والمرضعات. الكلمات: أطفال السودان الأمم ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Pledges Inclusive COP32 Process, Puts LDC Priorities At Center of Climate Agenda - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Pledges Inclusive COP32 Process, Puts LDC Priorities At Center of Climate Agenda 10 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Ethiopia reaffirmed its commitment to advancing the climate priorities of Least Developed Countries (LDCs), pledging an inclusive, transparent and collaborative process as it prepares to host the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) in Addis Ababa in November 2027. Foreign Affairs Minister and COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos reaffirmed the commitment during talks with LDC Group Chair Ambassador Adão Soares Barbosa of Timor-Leste at the Ethiopia Pavilion on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Gedion underscored the importance of close consultation and strong partnerships to ensure that the priorities, interests and perspectives of LDCs remain central to COP32 preparations and deliberations. He stressed that Ethiopia intends to work closely with the LDC Group and other international partners to build consensus and advance climate outcomes that reflect the shared aspirations of vulnerable countries. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The Minister also emphasized that a successful COP31 would provide a critical foundation for COP32, helping sustain momentum in global climate negotiations and deliver meaningful progress on collective climate action. Ethiopia is using its participation in COP31 to strengthen international partnerships, support constructive negotiations and build momentum for its upcoming presidency. Speaking on Monday, Gedion said Ethiopia's foremost priority at the Antalya conference is to contribute to a successful negotiation process that will lay a strong foundation for more effective outcomes at COP32. To this end, Ethiopia will work closely with the Turkish and Australian COP31 presidencies to support ongoing negotiations and facilitate a smooth and constructive transition to the next climate conference. Mobilizing international partnerships and building a shared understanding of Ethiopia's COP32 vision are also central to the country's engagement, he said, adding that the government is seeking to exchange perspectives, identify common interests and establish areas of cooperation with potential partners. Ethiopia also aims to use the global climate gathering to generate wider international interest in COP32 and encourage broad participation in the Addis Ababa summit. Gedion noted that the Ethiopia Pavilion is serving as a platform for dialogue, partnership-building and showcasing the country's climate initiatives, while offering international participants an early glimpse of Ethiopia's preparations and hospitality as the next COP host. ethiopia.title: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Reexamining Ethiopia's Ethnic Federal Model to Advance Peace and Security 10 November 2026 Africa Center for Strategic Studies (Washington, DC) By Joseph Siegle and Hany Wahila Reforming Ethiopia's ethnic federal model provides an opportunity to pivot away from the persistent instability generated by ethnic militias, though this will require opening political space as well as disarmament. Attacks launched by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies against the federal government in September 2026 raised fears of a return to the destructive conflict of 2020-2022, in which an estimated 600,000 people perished. While the federal government subsequently regained control over virtually all of the territories taken during the offensive, concerns persist that instability in northern Ethiopia could trigger a wider regional war--potentially colliding with the catastrophic conflict in Sudan and drawing in rival, well-resourced Gulf States. Overshadowed by these regional tensions are Ethiopia's ongoing domestic security challenges. The TPLF attacks were launched under the rubric of the so-called "Alliance for Survival"--comprised of a disparate coalition of seven Ethiopian armed groups: Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF) Benishangul People's Liberation Movement (BPLM) Gumuz People's Democratic Movement (GPDM) Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Representing dissident factions from their respective regions, the stated objective of the Alliance is to overthrow the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. While loosely organized (the alliance was declared just weeks before the September attacks), each of the seven groups had taken up arms against the government over the preceding years (and in some cases decades). Some were part of a precursor alliance formed in 2006 . The Ethiopian federal government's 2023 decision to integrate all regional militias under the federal army or police following the destructive Tigray conflict has met armed resistance from these and other militias, propelling an escalation in violent clashes in recent years. Fighting involving these groups and federal forces has resulted in an average of 1,500 clashes and 4,900 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024. Roughly 90 percent of these fatalities are linked to two groups: the Amhara Fano National Movement (60 percent) and the Oromo Liberation Army (30 percent). Left to fester, the threat from regional militias poses a deeper source of instability for the country. Ethiopia's ethnic federal model represents a source of structural instability. The militias' unwillingness to disarm and accept a unitary chain of command under the federal government exposes a structural defect in Ethiopia's ethnic federal model. Established by the TPLF-led federal government in 1995, the model created ethnically based jurisdictions and gave regions the right to secede. The constitution also authorized regional police forces, which have evolved into militarized special forces . Experience from other federal systems shows that ethnically based political jurisdictions and autonomous regional security forces contribute to fragmentation and increase the likelihood of conflict . Understanding the political, economic, and security drivers of Ethiopia's regional militias, therefore, can provide context for how the country addresses these persistent domestic security challenges and how it builds a federal governance structure that can be resilient and responsive to the diverse needs of Ethiopia's 135 million citizens. Tigray Region The political-security equation in Tigray is unique given the dominant role the TPLF held in national politics for nearly three decades. When the ruling Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Defense Forces (EPRDF) dissolved in 2019, the TPLF retained considerable political influence, experienced military commanders, and military assets. The unwillingness of the TPLF leadership to accede to federal authority set the stage for the 2020-2022 conflict. Even following the TPLF's 2022 defeat and the signing of the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement (COHA, also referred to as the Pretoria Agreement), hardliners in the TPLF, led by Debretsion Gebremichael, have attempted to undermine federal authority in Tigray. Debretsion was the former Minister of Communications and Information Technology and the Deputy Prime Minister in Ethiopia during EPRDF rule. Established under the COHA, the Tigray Interim Administration (TIA) was intended to facilitate the reintegration of Tigray into Ethiopia's federal structure. The TIA's authority, however, has been consistently challenged by the Debretsion-led faction of the TPLF, including the failure to give up heavy weapons as stipulated under COHA. This resistance grew more brazen over time, ultimately resulting in the TPLF unilaterally asserting the reinstatement of the pre-2022 regional council in April 2026. The majority of Tigray's citizens did not support the TPLF reigniting the conflict with the federal government. This power grab was rejected by many Tigrayans . A statement by the Salsay Weyane Tigray party in May 2026 captured these concerns: "For over three decades, this organization [the TPLF] has monopolized the politics of Tigray. It has now devolved into a tool for competing factions to seize power by force, making the gun the primary rule of the political game." This view was a recurring theme of a coalition of Tigrayan opposition parties that formed the Covenant for Radical Change in 2023, calling for political reforms in the region. TPLF hardliners were emboldened by an undeclared alliance with Eritrea that is believed to include access to weapons and deployment of Eritrean military forces in Tigray. This deepening belligerence culminated in a declaration of war and seizure of federal government assets in Tigray on September 23, 2026. Subsequent fighting with federal forces resulted in at least 277 battle-related fatalities. What becomes of the TPLF hardliners will be a central issue for the region moving forward. Given that the party has twice launched violent attacks on the federal government--at great cost in lives, economic loss, and regional stability--it has limited credibility as a democratic political actor. Rebuilding Tigray as part of Ethiopia's federal structure involves far more than the TPLF, however. Still recovering from the previous conflict, the majority of Tigray's 7.5 million citizens did not support the TPLF hardliners reigniting the conflict with the federal government. This limited support, underscored by the widespread evasion of the TPLF's forced conscription, is a key factor in the rapid collapse of the TPLF offensive in September and October 2026. The TPLF's short-lived territorial gains were also due to the creation of the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) in 2025. The TPF was formed by disaffected TPLF fighters who saw no future for themselves under the TPLF leadership and believed they should be defending Tigray rather than " preserving the same old elite ." The TPF contends that the Tigrayan military should be apolitical rather than aligned with one party. When fighting broke out in 2026, the TPF fought with the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) to repulse the TPLF offensive. Western Tigray A flashpoint in tensions between the Tigray and Amhara Regions is the status of Western Tigray (also known as Wolkayit). The jurisdiction was the focus of some of the most vicious violence during the 2020-2022 conflict, after which many Tigrayan residents were forced to flee the area and the land subsequently settled by Amhara communities. The region is the focus of competing territorial claims linked to iterative episodes of forced displacement and resettlement from previous eras. The COHA does not explicitly address the status of the area, and the federal government has called for a referendum by the territory's residents to resolve the matter. Tigrayans contend this solution would not account for the estimated 800,000 Tigrayans who have been displaced since 2020. The ongoing uncertainty and polarization around this issue have been a justification for militias in both Tigray and Amhara to retain their arms. After reclaiming the regional capital of Mekelle and other parts of Tigray, the federal authorities appointed a new TIA leadership, comprised of ethnic Tigrayans, in October. Their mandate is to oversee elections by April 2027, restore basic public services and infrastructure, and facilitate the return of displaced communities. Given the security challenges in the region, Tigrayans were unable to go to the polls during Ethiopia's general elections in June 2026. A participatory electoral process has the potential to redirect Tigrayan interests into institutionalized political channels--and undercut the rationale for violence. Some of the emerging political parties in Tigray include: Salsay Weyane Tigray Arena Tigray for Democracy and Sovereignty Tigray Democratic Solidarity National Congress of Great Tigray The varied political affiliations within Tigray underscore that the instability in the region has been largely driven by political rivalries. As in other political jurisdictions defined along ethnic boundaries , such structures provide a ready means to politicize ethnicity. Central issues will be how best to rebuild Tigray, provide basic services, facilitate the return of displaced populations, generate investment, and clarify the authorities of the regional administration. Given Tigray's location on the border with Sudan and Eritrea, security arrangements will be particularly critical. One of the sensitivities of the implementation of the COHA was that Eritrean forces never fully withdrew from some of Tigray's border districts. The extent to which this transition is perceived by Tigrayans as representative of their interests will have far-reaching implications for the stabilization of this turbulent region. Political stability, in turn, will contribute to economic reconstruction and foster stronger integration between Tigray and the much larger Ethiopian economy. Amhara Region With an estimated 33 million people, the Amhara Region is Ethiopia's second most populous and historically the most influential. Massive youth protests in the region facilitated the dissolution of the EPRDF in 2019. Animosities built up over the 30 years of TPLF control fueled Amhara's regional militias to fight alongside the ENDF during the 2020-2022 conflict. Some of these trained and experienced Amhara militias subsequently resisted the federal government's decision to dismantle all regional forces starting in April 2023. The leader of the Amhara Prosperity Party, Girma Yeshitila, was assassinated soon after the announcement . This sequence of events triggered a spike in violence between the decentralized Fano ("freedom fighter" in Amharic) militias and the regional and federal forces that has persisted across the Amhara Region ever since. Whereas the Amhara Region had been among the most stable in Ethiopia before the 2020-2022 conflict, it subsequently has faced some of the highest levels of violence, including approximately 3,500 battle-related fatalities annually since 2024. Fano's lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias' agenda or negotiation positions. Composed of former youth protesters, vigilantes, and special police forces, the Fano militias claim a mandate to protect the interests of ethnic Amharas . Some make more zealous demands of Amhara ethnic nationalism and territorial claims in neighboring regions, including Tigray. Still others advocate for a greater Ethiopian identity. Collectively, the Fano militias are estimated to have 15,000-20,000 fighters. Fano's lack of a cohesive political structure has impeded a clear articulation of the militias' agenda or negotiation positions. The merger of five Fano militias under the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) in January 2026 was viewed as a step toward a more formalized Fano structure. The AFNM's subsequent decision to sign onto the "Alliance for Survival," however, may undercut the group's ability to speak for the wider spectrum of Fano militias, most of which do not fall under the AFNM. The degree of popular support for the Fano militias is unclear. Some Fano militias have attempted to undermine the electoral process by intimidating citizens who sought to participate in the electoral process. As a result, voting did not take place in 8 of Amhara Region's 130 electoral districts. The ruling Prosperity Party claimed 117 seats in the House of People's Representatives 2026 election. In 2021, the Prosperity Party garnered 114 seats. The National Movement of Amhara (NaMA) secured six seats, and the Amhara Democratic Force Movement (ADFM) took three. The remaining seats were distributed among other parties, including the Ethiopians Citizens for Social Justice (EZEMA) party. Ethno-nationalist parties like the Argoba Unity Jeberti party are also active, though did not gain any seats. Roughly 90 percent of the fatalities linked to ethnic militias are tied to the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. NaMA alleges it has faced intimidation from federal authorities and several of the Party's elected members of parliament have been detained . In 2023, the Party's most vocal critic of the government, Christian Tadele , was charged with terrorism and possession of firearms. Despite Tadele's immunity, he was held in prison for over 3 years before being released in 2026 following a pardon. Between 80 and 90 percent of the population in Amhara rely on agriculture for their livelihoods. Incentivizing and scaling up investments to improve productivity and diversify the economy will depend on greater security in the region . Oromia Region Oromia is Ethiopia's most populous region with an estimated 43 million people. It is also one of the poorest and has not historically had significant representation at the federal level despite its relative proximity to the national capital Addis Ababa. Comprising roughly equal numbers of Muslims and Christians, Oromia has also been a focal point of periodic religious tensions . The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) was established in the 1970s as the armed wing of the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF) to advance Oromo self-determination. OLF leaders were forced into exile following a falling out with the TPLF-led transitional government in 1992, and the group was subsequently banned in 2008. Upon coming to power in 2018, Abiy signed a peace agreement with the OLF enabling its leadership to return. A faction of the OLA, however, refused to disarm , leading to a split from the OLF. While never commanding a large following, the OLA has been resilient. While never commanding a large following (the OLA is currently estimated to have 3,000 fighters), the OLA has been resilient. Following the federal government's 2023 decision to ban all armed militias, some splinter elements of the OLA did reach agreement with the regional authorities and gave up their arms. However, violence between the main OLA faction and the federal government has escalated. This has resulted in an average of roughly 1,200 annual battle-related fatalities since 2024, destabilizing parts of western Oromia where the OLA is most active. Even though it signed onto the Alliance for Survival, the OLA has yet to coordinate military operations with its alliance partners. The Oromo Prosperity Party dominates Oromia's representation in the House of People's Representatives, controlling 167 of the 178 available seats in the 2026 general elections. The remaining nine seats were won by unaffiliated opposition candidates. The two most prominent opposition parties in the region, the OLF and the Oromo Federalist Congress (OFC) party, did not gain any representation. As in 2021, the OFC did not contest the elections, lacking confidence in the fairness of the process. The OLF did campaign in the 2026 elections (after boycotting in 2021) yet failed to win a seat. The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA's continued attacks. The OLF has faced detention, harassment, and other restrictions that have impeded its ability to campaign. In April 2024, Bate Urgessa, an OLF spokesperson, was killed by an unknown attacker in Oromia 2 months after being detained for "conspiring to incite unrest" after speaking to a foreign journalist. The limited opposition representation has been used as a justification for the OLA's continued attacks. This includes blocking key roads and raids on foreign mining operations, demanding that extractive companies ensure local community beneficiation. An attack on the $340 million Tulu Kapi gold mine operated by UK-based KEFI Gold and Copper resulted in several fatalities and the suspension of mining operations. The OLF has called for negotiated settlements to end the clashes . They have called for proposals to establish a transitional national unity government in the Region to ensure representation and constructive engagement among opposition political parties and armed groups that have gone unrecognized by the ruling party. Ogaden, Benishangul, and Afar Regions Elements of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) have fought for greater autonomy of the Somali Region of Ethiopia since the 1977-1978 Ogaden War between Ethiopia and Somalia. Following the signing of a peace agreement with the federal government in 2018 as part of Abiy's reconciliation process, the majority of the ONLF disavowed armed struggle and has sought to represent the Somali Region's 13 million residents through political channels. Since signing the peace accords, the main Jijiga-faction of the ONLF has had its terrorist designation removed, re-registered as a political organization, disarmed and reintegrated most of its forces, and secured representation of 20 seats in the Regional Council during the last election cycle. The ONLF, accordingly, has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process. However, an old guard of the ONLF led by Abdirahman Mahadi has continued to mount guerrilla attacks against the federal government and is the faction that signed onto the Alliance for Survival. Comprised of an estimated several thousand fighters, the ONLF is linked to 111 reported fatalities in 2024, but less than 20 deaths since that time. The ONLF has been among the most successful parties to return from exile and engage in the political process. Comprising an estimated 1 million inhabitants, the Benishangul Region in northwest Ethiopia on the borders of Sudan and South Sudan is among the smallest in Ethiopia. The region is noteworthy for hosting the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). The Region has had armed groups intermittently fighting the federal government since the 1990s, claiming to represent indigenous ethnic groups. Despite various signed political settlements in 2005, 2012, and 2022, the Benishangul Peoples' Liberation Movement (BPLM) and Gumuz Peoples' Democratic Movement (GPDM) persist in their armed struggle largely from bases in Sudan's Blue Nile State, where they are reported to be supported by the Sudanese Armed Forces . Battle-related fatalities linked to these groups have increased in recent years from 10 in 2024 to 80 in 2026. The BPLM is one of the signatories to the Alliance for Survival. The Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (ARDUF), also known as Ugugumo, has engaged in armed struggle again
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia's ethnic federal model is under scrutiny as the country grapples with ongoing instability fueled by ethnic militias. Recent attacks by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) against the federal government have reignited fears of a return to the devastating conflict of 2020-2022, which resulted in approximately 600,000 deaths. The federal government's integration of regional militias into a unified force has met with resistance, leading to increased violence and fatalities, particularly involving the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. The ethnic federal model, established in 1995, has contributed to fragmentation and conflict due to its allowance for regional autonomy and armed forces. The TPLF's refusal to accept federal authority complicates efforts to stabilize Tigray, where a new interim administration faces challenges from hardliners. Addressing Ethiopia's security issues requires a comprehensive understanding of the political dynamics among its diverse ethnic groups and a commitment to reforming the federal governance structure.

The conference comes amid mounting reports of mass killings, religious persecution, widespread displacement, destruction of property, and continuing violence against innocent civilians across multiple regions of the country. At a time when Ethiopia faces escalating political instability, ethnic tensions, armed conflict, and a deepening humanitarian emergency, the conference will provide an important platform for human rights advocates, Ethiopian American community leaders, policymakers, and other concerned stakeholders to examine the deteriorating situation and call for meaningful international action. The conference will focus particularly on the suffering of civilians in the Amhara, Oromia—including Arsi and Wollega—and Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Reports of killings, abductions, attacks on religious institutions, destruction of homes, and other serious human rights violations underscore the urgent need for independent investigations, civilian protection, and accountability. Allegations of abuses involving government security forces, regional militias, and various armed groups must be examined impartially. No individual or institution should be above the law, and no civilian should become a target because of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or geographic identity. Ethiopia’s Humanitarian Catastrophe: Millions Displaced and Communities Devastated Ethiopia’s humanitarian emergency has reached alarming proportions. Humanitarian reporting indicated that more than 2.9 million people were internally displaced by late 2024, while more than 141,000 Ethiopian refugees were reported to be living outside the country. These figures demonstrate the enormous human cost of prolonged conflict, insecurity, and political instability. The crisis has continued to evolve in 2026, with additional displacement reported in conflict-affected communities. Since September 2026, reports of intensified violence in the Amhara region have raised further concerns, including claims of more than one million additional people displaced. These figures require independent verification, but the reported scale of suffering demands immediate attention. Behind every displacement figure is a human tragedy. Families have been separated, children have lost access to education, farmers have abandoned their land, and entire communities have been forced to flee their homes. Many displaced families struggle to obtain food, clean water, healthcare, shelter, and basic protection. Hospitals and other essential public infrastructure have reportedly been damaged or destroyed in conflict-affected areas. Medical personnel, patients, and humanitarian workers face significant obstacles in reaching vulnerable populations. The destruction of healthcare facilities, combined with food insecurity and restricted humanitarian access, has further intensified civilian suffering. The humanitarian crisis in Ethiopia deserves the same seriousness and international attention afforded to other major global emergencies. The suffering of millions of Ethiopians must not be overlooked simply because other international conflicts dominate the headlines. Government Responsibility and the Protection of Civilians The Ethiopian government has a fundamental constitutional and moral responsibility to protect the lives, safety, religious freedom, and property of all its citizens, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation, or geographic location. This responsibility includes preventing attacks against civilians, maintaining public security, protecting religious institutions, ensuring humanitarian access, investigating credible reports of human rights violations, and holding those responsible accountable through fair and independent legal proceedings. The government cannot dismiss this responsibility or shift it entirely to regional authorities and other political actors. Protecting innocent civilians is among the most fundamental obligations of any government. The international community should continue pressing Ethiopian authorities and all armed actors to fulfill their obligations and ensure that civilians are protected. Ethnic Federalism and the Erosion of National Unity One of the central issues expected to receive considerable attention at the December 11 conference is the impact of Ethiopia’s ethnic-based federal system on national unity, political stability, and the protection of fundamental human rights. Critics of ethnic federalism argue that the system has institutionalized ethnic divisions, weakened national cohesion, and contributed to a political environment in which ethnic identity increasingly influences political representation, access to security, and relations between communities. Rather than creating a genuinely inclusive political system, the framework has, according to its critics, deepened divisions and contributed to recurring cycles of political confrontation, insecurity, and violence. The consequences have been particularly devastating for civilians in Amhara and Oromia, where communities have experienced repeated attacks, displacement, and insecurity. Ethiopia needs a political and constitutional framework that guarantees equal citizenship and protects the fundamental rights of every Ethiopian. National unity must not require the suppression of cultural, linguistic, or religious diversity. Instead, diversity should be protected within a democratic system founded on equality, individual rights, constitutional guarantees, and the rule of law. The conference will provide an opportunity to discuss comprehensive constitutional reform, inclusive political dialogue, and the development of independent institutions that serve all Ethiopians equally. Mass Killings and the Persecution of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians Among the most disturbing aspects of Ethiopia’s human rights crisis are reports of continuing attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Christians, including targeted killings, attacks on places of worship, and the destruction and burning of religious institutions. Reports emerging from Arsi, Wollega, and other parts of Oromia have described horrific attacks against Orthodox Christian communities. In several reported incidents, civilians have allegedly been targeted because of their religious identity, while churches, homes, and other religious properties have been attacked or destroyed. The suffering of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians cannot be separated from the broader human rights crisis affecting the country. Religious persecution, ethnic violence, and political instability have become interconnected challenges that demand immediate attention. The Ethiopian government has a constitutional and moral obligation to protect religious freedom and ensure the safety of every religious community. The protection of churches, mosques, monasteries, clergy, worshippers, and other religious institutions must be guaranteed under the law. Repeated attacks, coupled with concerns about inadequate investigations and the absence of accountability, raise serious questions about the effectiveness of existing security and law enforcement mechanisms. The deliberate targeting of civilians because of their religious or ethnic identity must never be tolerated. The international community should take seriously credible warnings of potentially genocidal violence and support impartial investigations into allegations of mass atrocities. Religious freedom is a fundamental human right, not a privilege granted by political authorities. Transitional Justice Without Accountability Is Not Justice Another important issue is Ethiopia’s transitional justice process, which was presented as a mechanism for addressing past atrocities, promoting reconciliation, and establishing accountability. However, serious concerns remain regarding transparency, independence, inclusiveness, and the implementation of meaningful reforms. A transitional justice process cannot succeed if victims and affected communities are excluded, perpetrators remain unaccountable, or investigations are influenced by political considerations. Justice must be applied equally, regardless of ethnicity, political affiliation, religious identity, or government position. Ethiopia needs an independent and credible accountability mechanism capable of investigating serious violations committed by all parties to the conflict. Victims and survivors must have meaningful opportunities to participate in the process, and those responsible for serious crimes must face appropriate legal consequences. Without accountability, reconciliation becomes an empty promise. Sustainable peace cannot be built on impunity, selective justice, or the deliberate exclusion of affected communities. The Responsibility of the United States and the International Community The December 11 Congressional conference will also examine the important role the United States can play in encouraging a peaceful, democratic, and stable future for Ethiopia. The United States has historically maintained significant diplomatic, economic, and security relationships with Ethiopia. These relationships provide Washington with considerable diplomatic influence and opportunities to encourage respect for human rights, civilian protection, democratic governance, and political reform. Under President Donald Trump, the administration and Congress should give renewed attention to Ethiopia’s deteriorating humanitarian and security situation. Addressing this crisis should be viewed not only as a human rights priority but also as an important component of U.S. policy toward the Horn of Africa. Congressional leadership and bipartisan engagement are particularly important. Members of the House and Senate should consider stronger oversight, bipartisan legislative initiatives, targeted sanctions against individuals credibly implicated in serious human rights violations, and appropriate conditions on U.S. assistance. Such measures should be carefully designed to promote accountability without worsening the suffering of ordinary Ethiopians. The United States should also work closely with the United Nations, African Union, European Union, and regional partners to advance the following priorities: Immediate Protection of Civilians: Press the Ethiopian government and all armed actors to end attacks against civilians and protect vulnerable communities. Independent Investigations: Support credible and impartial investigations into reported mass killings, religious persecution, forced displacement, and other serious human rights violations. Expanded Humanitarian Assistance: Improve access to emergency food, medicine, shelter, and healthcare for displaced populations and communities affected by conflict. Accountability and Justice: Pursue appropriate consequences for individuals responsible for atrocities and ensure that transitional justice mechanisms are independent, transparent, and inclusive. Inclusive National Dialogue: Encourage a genuinely inclusive political process involving all major stakeholders, including representatives of Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, and other Ethiopian communities. Democratic and Constitutional Reform: Support fundamental freedoms, religious liberty, freedom of expression, independent media, judicial independence, and free and credible elections. Stronger International Diplomatic Engagement: Strengthen U.S. diplomatic leadership in the Horn of Africa and coordinate efforts with regional and international institutions to prevent further destabilization. The United States should use its diplomatic relationships and international partnerships to encourage a peaceful political process that addresses the underlying causes of Ethiopia’s conflicts. Ethiopia’s Crisis Is a Threat to Regional Stability Ethiopia is strategically important to the Horn of Africa and the African continent. Its continued instability carries consequences extending well beyond its national borders. The country’s conflicts and humanitarian emergency have contributed to population displacement and placed additional pressure on neighboring countries, including Sudan and Kenya. Continued instability also threatens regional security, economic development, cross-border cooperation, and the broader interests of the international community. With a population exceeding 120 million, Ethiopia is one of Africa’s most strategically significant countries. Its stability is essential not only to the well-being of its citizens but also to the long-term security and economic development of the Horn of Africa. The international community cannot afford to wait until the crisis becomes even more difficult to contain. Preventive diplomacy, inclusive political engagement, and sustained international attention are urgently needed. Ethiopian Americans Urge African Union to Include Amhara People in Ethiopia’s Peace Process The importance of an inclusive political process was also emphasized in a recent interview with Channel Africa, during which Ethiopian American civic advocates discussed their appeal to African Union Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf. The Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations called on the African Union to support an inclusive and sustainable peace process that gives the Amhara people and all major stakeholders a meaningful voice in discussions concerning Ethiopia’s future. The advocates expressed concern that the Pretoria Agreement was limited to its signatories, while other conflicts, civilian suffering, displacement, and serious human rights concerns continued across Ethiopia. Their appeal to the African Union emphasized four important priorities: Inclusion of the Amhara people and all major stakeholders in peace negotiations. Protection of civilians and religious freedom. Impartial investigations and accountability for human rights violations. Meaningful national dialogue addressing the underlying causes of conflict. As emphasized during the interview, military action alone cannot deliver lasting peace. Ethiopia needs inclusive dialogue, justice, accountability, and genuine national reconciliation. Channel Africa Interview: Listen to the interview: Ethiopian Americans Call on the African Union to Ensure Amhara Inclusion in Ethiopia’s Peace Process A Call to Action: Ethiopian Americans Must Make Their Voices Heard The December 11 Congressional conference represents an important opportunity to bring the voices and concerns of suffering Ethiopians directly to policymakers in Washington. For Ethiopian Americans, this is more than a political discussion. It is a humanitarian responsibility and a commitment to defending the fundamental rights, dignity, and lives of innocent civilians in their homeland. Ethiopian Americans are taxpayers, constituents, and active members of American society. They have every right to ask their elected representatives to pay attention to the suffering of millions of people in Ethiopia and to use America’s diplomatic influence to encourage meaningful change. Community participation and sustained advocacy are essential. Ethiopian Americans should continue contacting their representatives in Congress, sharing credible reports, supporting independent human rights documentation, and encouraging bipartisan action. Accurate information is equally important. The international community cannot respond effectively without reliable reporting, independent documentation, and the willingness of human rights advocates, journalists, religious leaders, and affected communities to speak openly about atrocities. Silence and indifference risk allowing impunity to flourish and further violence to continue. Ethiopia deserves a future built on democratic governance, equal citizenship, constitutional protections, religious freedom, national reconciliation, and respect for human dignity. No ethnic group, religious community, or political constituency should be left vulnerable to violence or denied equal protection under the law. The United States Congress, the Trump administration, and the international community must recognize that protecting innocent civilians is not optional. It is a fundamental responsibility under international human rights principles. The December 11 Conference: An Opportunity for Meaningful Action The December 11 Congressional conference on Capitol Hill is an opportunity to move beyond expressions of concern and toward concrete policy recommendations and sustained international engagement. The conference seeks to elevate the experiences of victims and affected communities, encourage bipartisan Congressional attention, and advance practical measures to protect civilians, promote accountability, and support an inclusive political process. The central message is clear: Ethiopia’s human rights and humanitarian crisis must no longer be ignored. The lives and dignity of innocent Ethiopians matter. The time for meaningful international engagement, accountability, and the protection of civilian lives is now. Ethiopia needs peace, justice, democracy, and equal protection for all its citizens. The international community must act before more innocent lives are lost. ethiopia.content: Kenya: Tens of Thousands Flee Into Kenya As Clashes Erupt in Ethiopia's Moyale - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Kenya: Tens of Thousands Flee Into Kenya As Clashes Erupt in Ethiopia's Moyale 10 November 2026 Radio France Internationale By RFI Humanitarian groups in Moyale in northern Kenya are calling for urgent funding to support tens of thousands of people who have fled violent clashes in southern Ethiopia. About 50,000 people have crossed into the Kenyan side of Moyale, a border town straddling northern Kenya and southern Ethiopia , where many are struggling to find food, water and shelter. "Families who fled are facing serious shortages of food, water and adequate shelter, while the communities hosting them already have limited resources," said Nomagugu Ncube , Kenya chief of mission for the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM). Hosts under strain Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Most of the displaced are staying with relatives or members of the local community, which puts pressure on food and water supplies that were already scarce. Others have taken refuge in schools and temporary sites, and some are sleeping outdoors. The displacement follows renewed violence linked to a long-running dispute between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions over land and administrative control. On 18 October, a Somali flag was raised at an administrative office in Ethiopia's Moyale, a city jointly administered by the two regions. This triggered an exchange of gunfire between local militias in which a 13-year-old girl was killed, sparking protests and further violence. Thousands flee The fighting spread across seven districts, leaving more than a dozen people dead and forcing tens of thousands to flee, many of them across the border into Kenya . The Kenyan government is working with the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, to register new arrivals and assess their needs. Other humanitarian organisations, including the Kenya Red Cross, are also providing aid. The Kenya Red Cross initially put the number of displaced people at 36,000. The IOM has since raised its estimate to 50,000, but the figure could rise further as assessments continue, and no comprehensive official count is yet available. Approximately 50,000 individuals have crossed the border, facing severe shortages of food, water, and shelter. The Kenyan government, in collaboration with the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and other humanitarian organizations like the Kenya Red Cross, is working to register new arrivals and assess their needs. As assessments continue, the number of displaced individuals may rise further.

Leading Ethiopia's delegation at the Eighth WTO Working Party meeting in Geneva on November 9-10, Minister of Trade and Regional Integration and Chief Negotiator Yasmin Wahabrebbi, alongside State Minister of Foreign Affairs Ambassador Hadera Abera and other senior officials, underscored WTO membership as a top national priority. The renewed momentum follows the formation of a new government in October and comes as Ethiopia accelerates economic reforms to advance an accession process launched in 2003. Addressing the meeting, Minister Yasmin highlighted the progress achieved in aligning the country's legal and regulatory frameworks with WTO requirements, including the review of more than 460 legal instruments, the submission of updated accession documents and the implementation of wide-ranging trade-related reforms. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn She also reaffirmed Ethiopia's readiness to conclude bilateral market access negotiations, while calling on WTO members to adopt a flexible and development-sensitive approach that recognizes the country's economic circumstances and development priorities. WTO Deputy Director-General Xiangchen Zhang and member states welcomed Ethiopia's reform progress, expressing support for bringing the country's market of more than 130 million people into the multilateral trading system. The two-day meeting is expected to address outstanding multilateral issues, accelerate negotiations and establish a clearer pathway toward the conclusion of Ethiopia's accession process. For Ethiopia, WTO membership represents more than entry into a global trade institution. It is a strategic step toward strengthening export competitiveness, attracting investment, expanding market opportunities and improving the country's participation in international trade. It is also expected to reinforce Ethiopia's broader regional economic integration, including through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), as the country pursues a more competitive and outward-oriented economy. Minister Yasmin called on WTO members to match Ethiopia's political commitment and reform efforts with a pragmatic and constructive negotiating approach, stressing the importance of reaching a mutually beneficial outcome. In interviews with ENA on the sidelines of the African Political Party Summit, Douglas Togara Mwonzora of Zimbabwe and Irene Mphahama of Lesotho highlighted Ethiopia's development strides, natural resource management and efforts to expand women's participation in leadership. The delegates also called on African political parties to move beyond electoral competition and work collectively to advance development, strengthen democratic institutions and accelerate continental prosperity. Mwonzora, President of Zimbabwe's Movement for Democratic Change, praised Ethiopia's hospitality, expanding infrastructure and clean urban environment, saying the progress witnessed by his delegation demonstrated Africa's capacity to drive development through effective mobilization of its own resources. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "The infrastructure is good, the city is extremely clean, and we are very happy about that," he said. He particularly highlighted Ethiopia's experience in managing and harnessing natural resources for national development, noting that Zimbabwe, which possesses considerable mineral wealth, could draw valuable lessons from the country's development approach. Mwonzora stressed that Africa's natural resources should serve as engines of shared prosperity rather than sources of conflict or wealth concentrated in the hands of political elites. "Natural resources should be transformed from a curse to a blessing," he said, emphasizing the importance of responsible resource management for the benefit of citizens. Turning to the role of political parties, he urged both governing and opposition parties to recognize development as a common national and continental responsibility rather than allowing political competition to undermine progress. "Political parties should be the drivers of development in Africa--both ruling parties and the opposition," he stated. He also emphasized the importance of consensus on electoral rules, respect for constitutional principles and sustained political cooperation beyond elections to promote stability and accountability. Meanwhile, Irene Mphahama of Lesotho identified Ethiopia's progress in women's leadership and urban development as particularly valuable lessons from her visit. She said her interactions with Ethiopia's Minister of Women had provided insights into women's participation in decision-making, expressing her intention to share the experience and promote greater female representation in leadership back home. "I have to implement this and share it with the rest of the women in Lesotho," she said. Mphahama, who works in the construction sector, also praised Ethiopia's urban transformation and the pace of infrastructure development, describing them as evidence of strong development ambition and commitment. Recalling her visit to a river development project in Ethiopia, she said the transformation demonstrated how determination, planning and commitment could turn development aspirations into tangible results. "From that small project alone, we learn that you can do it. If you put your mind to it, you can do it," she emphasized. In a statement issued Tuesday, Nov. 10, Somalia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation expressed sympathy to the Egyptian government and the families of those killed in the accident. “Somalia stands in solidarity with brotherly Egypt at this difficult time. We pray that Allah grants mercy to those who lost their lives and patience to their families, and we wish the injured a swift and full recovery,” the statement said. advertisements The collision occurred Nov. 8 in the al-Ayyat district of Giza province, approximately 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of Cairo. According to Egyptian railway authorities, a passenger train traveling from Giza to Fayoum crashed into the rear of another train traveling from Cairo to Aswan, causing several carriages to derail. Egypt's Health Ministry confirmed that seven people were killed and 125 others injured in the accident. Emergency responders deployed 72 ambulances to evacuate casualties, while rescue teams and railway workers worked to remove damaged carriages and restore services. The injured were transported to hospitals in Giza and neighboring areas, where medical teams provided emergency treatment. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi expressed condolences to the families of the victims and ordered an urgent investigation into the collision. He directed authorities to determine the circumstances surrounding the accident and hold anyone found responsible for negligence accountable. Egyptian prosecutors launched an investigation, while railway officials deployed technical teams to examine the damaged trains and tracks. Witnesses described chaotic scenes following the collision, with local residents joining emergency personnel to help passengers trapped inside damaged carriages. Egyptian National Railways said services on the affected route were restored Monday after crews cleared the wreckage and repaired damaged tracks. somalia.title: Somalia and Somaliland’s Spiral of Mutual Destruction - Geeska
somalia.content: Somalia and Somaliland’s Spiral of Mutual Destruction | Geeska Skip to main content Wednesday 11 November 2026 EN AR SO EN AR SO Home Current Analysis Opinion Culture Files Newsletter Multimedia Interviews Opinion Somalia and Somaliland’s Spiral of Mutual Destruction 11 November, 2026 Image Abdullahi Hussein Born of a voluntary union, Somalia and Somaliland have become locked in a contest for diplomatic leverage, drawing Ethiopia, Türkiye, Israel and Saudi Arabia into their rivalry. As each seeks to constrain the other, both risk surrendering influence over their own security, resources and political future. Somaliland and Somalia united voluntarily in 1960 around a shared pan-Somali irredentist project. What began as a partnership has hardened into a rivalry in which each seeks external backing, making concessions over sovereignty and natural resources in an effort to counter the other. Their confrontation increasingly resembles mutually assured destruction (MAD): each move triggers a countermove, leaving both weaker and with less room to act independently. Understanding this trajectory requires examining the flawed foundations of their union and the sharply divergent paths they followed after the collapse of the Somali Republic. A Union Built on Sand When British Somaliland gained independence on 26 June 1960, followed five days later by Italian Somalia, Somaliland chose to unite with its newly independent neighbour to form the Somali Republic. The union reflected the Greater Somalia project, which sought to bring Somali-inhabited territories, including Djibouti, the Ogaden and Kenya’s Northern Frontier District, under a single sovereign state. Its legal basis was disputed from the outset: the Act of Union adopted by Somaliland’s parliament was not ratified by Somalia’s parliament in accordance with legal requirements. In a June 1961 referendum, northern voters rejected the proposed constitution, having already experienced marginalisation in political appointments and the allocation of resources within the new republic. Somaliland and Somalia united voluntarily in 1960 around a shared pan-Somali irredentist project. What began as a partnership has hardened into a rivalry in which each seeks external backing, making concessions over sovereignty and natural resources in an effort to counter the other. The imbalance deepened after Major General Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in October 1969, suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament and abolished the Supreme Court. The regime’s brutality in 1988, including the aerial bombardment of Hargeisa and Burao, was documented by Africa Watch and the United Nations as a campaign of genocide against the Isaaq clan . The violence destroyed any remaining basis for union. By the time the regime collapsed in January 1991, many in the north no longer wished to remain part of it. What followed from 1991 was one of the sharpest political divergences on the African continent. After declaring the dissolution of the Act of Union in May that year, Somaliland pursued indigenous, bottom-up processes of peacebuilding and state-building. Clan elders convened major community conferences, notably in Burao in 1991 and Borama in 1993, to establish a transitional charter and negotiate disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) arrangements through which militias were disarmed and former combatants integrated into national security forces. Voters ratified a constitution establishing multiparty democracy in 2001. Somaliland subsequently held presidential, parliamentary and local council elections that international observers described as credible and competitive. In the 2010 presidential election, President Dahir Riyale conceded defeat to Ahmed Silanyo of the opposition Kulmiye party. In 2024, President Muse Bihi Abdi likewise transferred power peacefully to his political rival, Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi (Irro), of the opposition Waddani party—a rarity in Africa and the Arab world. Somalia followed a different path. Since 1991, the international community has sponsored more than 14 peace conferences in Addis Ababa, Cairo, Nairobi and Djibouti, but these efforts have not produced durable governance . Despite substantial international support and successive African Union peacekeeping missions—AMISOM, ATMIS and AUSSOM—Somalia has struggled to provide security across the country. Al-Shabaab, an al-Qaeda-affiliated insurgency that emerged in 2006, continues to control significant territory and carry out attacks in and around Mogadishu. The contrast between the two entities is not accidental; it reflects the legitimacy and social rootedness of each political project. The Cost of Foreign Alliances The problem is not simply that Somaliland and Somalia have failed to reunite or agree on separation. It is that both have drawn external powers into the dispute, sacrificing sovereign assets for geopolitical leverage. The resulting competition risks weakening both sides while giving their external partners greater influence over their choices. Economic pressure was one source of this escalation. As early as 2023, Mogadishu began seeking to tax livestock exports through Berbera and claim a share of revenue collected by Somaliland. It also sought to enlist Saudi Arabia as a third party to pressure Somaliland into rejoining the union by restricting direct livestock exports to the kingdom. Somalia neither controls nor administers Berbera, yet the dispute over taxes and exports disrupted trade and threatened livelihoods across Somaliland. Somaliland has gained recognition from Israel, but not broad international recognition, while Somalia has not brought Somaliland back into the union. Both remain exposed to outside pressure and have less freedom to set the terms of their own security and economic relationships. Against this backdrop, Somaliland President Muse Bihi Abdi signed a memorandum of understanding with Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on 1 January 2024. The agreement brought together Ethiopia’s search for access to the sea and Somaliland’s pursuit of recognition. It provided for Ethiopia to lease coastal land for a naval and commercial facility in exchange for Ethiopia’s recognition of Somaliland’s statehood and equity in Ethiopian state enterprises. Ethiopia, with a population of about 120 million, is the world’s most populous landlocked country. Crisis Group described the agreement as a “port-for-recognition swap”: an arrangement that served both sides’ interests but heightened regional tensions. Somalia responded by recalling its ambassador to Addis Ababa, convening emergency multilateral summits and passing a parliamentary bill declaring the memorandum “null and void”. Mogadishu also strengthened its relationship with Türkiye, signing a maritime and defence agreement in early 2024, followed by an oil and gas cooperation deal. The defence agreement gave Türkiye a significant role in supporting Somalia’s maritime security; reports also described an exchange involving access to the blue economy. In January 2025, Villa Somalia reportedly granted Yemeni-born Saudi businessman Mohammed Qaid Saeed, known as Abu Yasir, exclusive rights over Somalia’s livestock export sector, including Berbera. Somaliland’s livestock minister condemned the move as “an attack on the polity’s economy and independence” and announced a four-day suspension of livestock exports. Traders reported that more than 80,000 animals were stranded at Berbera port. Sahan Global also reported that Abu Yasir had been accused in 2010 of planting a false story in a Saudi newspaper alleging inadequate animal-health inspections at Berbera. The reported monopoly extended Mogadishu’s economic pressure to a port it did not govern. In July 2025, Prime Minister Hamza Ali Barre described the political and security costs of the diplomatic campaign against the memorandum in a video statement : “ For a complete one year we haven't done anything else other than to wage diplomatic war to defend our sovereignty. That resulted in the terror group Al-Shabaab to retake the land that was previously liberated from them, because our attention was consumed by the fight with the MOU. There may be other MOUs that we may not know ”. He linked the government’s focus on the memorandum to al-Shabaab’s recapture of previously liberated territory. The dispute widened further when Somaliland accepted mutual recognition from Israel on 26 December 2025, alongside an agreement to establish full diplomatic relations and cooperate on defence. Israel became the first state to recognise Somaliland , while Somalia condemned the decision as a violation of its territorial integrity. Israel’s ambassador presented credentials in Hargeisa on 2 November 2026. Saudi Arabia also became more directly involved in support of Mogadishu. Calabrese (2026) links Riyadh’s position to its strategic interests in the Red Sea corridor and reports that the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation condemned Israel’s recognition as a threat to peace and security in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. On 9 February 2026, Saudi Arabia and Somalia formalised their alignment in a military cooperation memorandum. What began as a dispute over livestock exports and expanded through the Ethiopia–Somaliland memorandum has drawn Ethiopia, Türkiye, Israel and Saudi Arabia into the rivalry, each supporting one side in different ways. A framework of peaceful coexistence—shared management of security threats, open trade through Berbera and free movement across a de facto border—would cost both parties far less than the accumulating losses of their current course. The costs of this rivalry are not identical, but neither side has escaped them. Both have made strategic concessions to external powers whose interests may not always align with their own. Somalia has deepened its maritime and resource agreements with Türkiye; Somaliland has accepted greater exposure to regional tensions through its relationship with Israel. Somaliland has gained recognition from Israel, but not broad international recognition, while Somalia has not brought Somaliland back into the union. Both remain exposed to outside pressure and have less freedom to set the terms of their own security and economic relationships. The Case for Coexistence A more rational equilibrium is available and demonstrably achievable. Djibouti was one of the five Somali-inhabited territories that the original Somali Republic sought to incorporate into Greater Somalia. It chose independence in 1977 and today maintains positive relations with Mogadishu, including by hosting the Djibouti Process peace conferences of 2000 and 2008 . There is therefore no structural reason why Somaliland and Somalia could not pursue a similar relationship. A framework of peaceful coexistence—shared management of security threats, open trade through Berbera and free movement across a de facto border—would cost both parties far less than the accumulating losses of their current course. More than 35 years without agreement on reunification or formal separation have allowed the dispute to deepen. The costs are visible in the resources committed to competing diplomatic campaigns, the growing involvement of regional powers and the continuing threat from al-Shabaab. Cooperation would not resolve every disagreement, but both sides have much to lose by continuing to put leverage ahead of accommodation.
